content: Psychological complications are frequently observed in individuals who have experienced a stroke. These complications often result in a lack of motivation to engage in daily living activities. Motivational interviewing is a structured therapeutic approach aimed at enhancing intrinsic motivation, which may potentially improve the ability of stroke survivors to perform activities of daily living. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of motivational interviewing in improving activities of daily living among stroke survivors. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Stroke Group's Trials Register (as of November 2014), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; 2015, Issue 1), MEDLINE (1948 to March 2015), EMBASE (1980 to March 2015), CINAHL (1982 to March 2015), AMED (1985 to March 2015), PsycINFO (1806 to March 2015), PsycBITE (March 2015), and four Chinese databases. Additional efforts were made to identify relevant studies by searching ongoing trial registries, reviewing conference proceedings, examining reference lists, and contacting authors of pertinent studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared motivational interviewing with no intervention, sham motivational interviewing, or other psychological therapies in individuals who had experienced a stroke. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, extracted relevant data, and assessed the risk of bias. The primary outcomes measured included activities of daily living, mood, and mortality. Only one study, involving 411 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This study compared motivational interviewing with usual care. The findings did not demonstrate significant differences between the groups in terms of independence in activities of daily living or mortality rates at three-month and 12-month follow-ups. However, participants who received motivational interviewing were more likely to exhibit a normal mood compared to those who received usual care at both three-month and 12-month follow-ups. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of motivational interviewing as a means to improve activities of daily living in stroke survivors. They emphasized the need for further well-designed randomized controlled trials to better evaluate the efficacy of this intervention.
